SKA unveils Antenna two - 2015

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
SKA is the best news in SA today, our scientists and engineers are doing us proud, ensuring we lead the international community with the most advance radio telescope facility in the world

Summary:
Now we have won the bid and the politics of SKA have settled what has happened over the last year? The construction of the radio telescopes on Meerkat has begun on the back of what we learnt with the Kat 7 array. The 2nd Meerkat radio telescope is in place and the 3rd is under construction. Our design and construction of the telescopes has been so cost effective and advanced that massive funding has come into South Africa for the construction of the next 61. The Big Data, 1000 terabytes a year which the 64 antenna Meerkat array will generate, requires a slew of astrophysicist and data technicians to process this data. In the light of this massive opportunity over 600 grants have been created to ensure we have the requisite skills to keep it local.

Further information:
The second Meerkat radio telescope is up and the 3rd is under construction, with 61 more on the way. Meerkat will be the most powerful radio telescope in the world and forms part of phase one of SKA. There is no blueprint for these radio telescopes and as scientists and astronomers configure their requirements, the engineers have to come up with the plans on how to construct them in the most cost-effective manner. So far they have done such an excellent and cost-effective job that the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy in Bonn has made R150 million available for South Africa to build and install them. MeerKAT is expected to do transformational science on pulsars and other areas of astronomy, and despite the fact it has only two telescopes up, it has already been used by scientists from around the world.
The construction and erection of these telescopes has opened up whole new career paths for local electrical engineering technicians, and the telescopes are now being operated and maintained by a slew of new technicians, freeing the scientists to get on with the work they were trained for.
Until recently, the University of the Western Cape had just one post-graduate physicist, now it boasts a whole astronomy department headed up by Professors Russ Taylor and Roy Maartens. They are ensuring that we have the requisite skilled personnel – astrophysicists and data scientists inside South Africa to handle the 1000 terabytes of data which will be gathered per year when the full Meerkat array is up. This phenomenon, known as Big Data, needs astronomers, computer scientists, and mathematicians to decipher it accurately. UWC and universities throughout South Africa now have the funding to develop this capacity locally to ensure it is not outsourced to international service providers.
The latest science coming out of the Meerkat telescopes was announced today by UWC and is part of an international cosmology study. They have devised a way of using the Meerkat Radio telescopes to map the radiation from hydrogen atoms to form a 3D map of the universe. These 3D maps will be able to test the limits of General Relativity and the origins of the universe. They can start testing their theories using data gathered from the antennae already in place and expand as the full array is completed. SKA is set to be a giant physics lab for scientists around the world.
This insert will also look at what impact some of the technological and engineering advances and data gathered will have on our day to day lives. These advances do not only benefit our understanding of the universe and dark matter, but have practical and commercial implications for our everyday lives.

Press Release:


SKA
Top scientists the world over are lining up to be part of South Africa’s Square Kilometre Array radio telescope project and the cutting edge in global astronomy. Hidden deep in the Karoo, Carte Blanche gets exclusive access to the site and an unprecedented take on a 650 million euro project that is set to plot a 3D map of the universe like never before.


Script:


Script: Hidden deep in the Karoo, as far as possible from radio interference, and therefore humans, lie the beginnings of the world’s biggest radio telescope, the Square kilometre array or SKA. It’s a 10 hour road trip from Cape Town, but we got lucky, and caught the weekly flight with some of the top scientific minds from all over the world.
Justin Jonas- Derek 02 49 00 18 I mean you are quite fussy out here, cellphones and ipads left in the plane, is it all necessary
Justin “Absolutely for two reasons one is to protect our equipment if we were sitting here with a cellphone near the receiver we could destroy in the order of a R100 000 worth of equipment if you were further away with your cellphone that would interfere with the data that would be collected and the scientists would be after you
Script: Professor Justin Jonas, Associate Director for Science and Engineering of SKA SA, has been leading the scientific team for the last 10 years. He says radio telescopes allow us to see far more of the universe as they penetrate the cosmic dust. Radio and optical telescopes see opposite sides of the same picture, and when combined we see the full image.
LINK 02 13 18 15 A mere 7 years ago this was Jan Louw’s sheep farm. Now it is the epicentre of the world’s largest science experiment looking back at the cradle of life
Script: It started out with the 7 Karoo Array Telescopes, Kat 7
Justin Jonas 03 10 49 The idea of Kat 7 was really to prove to the rest of the world that we could build something in SA here in the site and also to develop the science and engineering skills that we needed. But it has morphed now into a scientific instrument with its own life and is oversubscribed by the international community so we would have perhaps have thought that it would have been mothballed while we were building Meerkat but it is in fact running 24/7 science operations and published papers in top journals around the world
Script: Meerkat is the next phase of the project and literally means more Kat.
Justin Jonas 02 53 29 So Meerkat is 64 dishes and that is our SA funded program following on from that is SKA phase one which is of the order of 250 dishes …that’s including the Meerkat dishes and then further into the future, probably 2030 or so, SKA 2 where there maybe 2500 dishes but off course not just in this area they would be spread all over Africa they are extending out to as far as Ghana and the Indian ocean islands
LINK 02 16 50 17 They say it’s not just about where we have come from, it’s where we are going to and the SKA is being built for people who are not yet born to answer questions we haven’t even thought of
Script: Director Dr Bernie Fanaroff, is delighted that the telescopes are already “doing science”, even although the full array is not in place.
Bernie Fanaroff 06 53 58 what the SKA will be doing is really making a very detailed map of the universe so you can look back to the very earliest of times before there were any stars or galaxies in the universe when it was filled with cold and dark hydrogen gas and then watch how the stars form and the galaxies form and you will be able to watch how that develops through 13 and half billion years up to present time
Script: Leading Cosmologist, Professor Mario Santos, has just published some of the first papers detailing how they plan to do 3d mapping of the universe
Mario 03 23 00 06 . Strange questions like what is this dark energy that makes 70% of our universe can be answered by making these maps and seeing how they evolve
Derek 03 23 37 what is this dark energy?
Mario Ha ha know no one knows it is the most amazing question in cosmology now
Script: In 2012, South Africa won the site bid to co-host SKA with Australia. South Africa will look at a small patch of the sky in great detail and Australia will look at a large piece of the sky in less detail.
Derek “So what’s happened since you got the bid ?”
Justin Jonas 03 05 33 -----So the SKA office has been formed there is a legal entity now in the world that represents the SKA and we are working with their staff to establish the SKA presence here on site. At the moment this is still a SA Meerkat site and it will evolve across to being the SKA site in Africa.
Script: The first two Meerkat dishes are up and in June they start producing 3 a month. By the end of 2016 there will be 64 dishes in place
Bernie Fanaroff 06 53 12 we are testing the new receivers that have been built by local SA industry and they are working about 3 times as well as we specified, so in effect the Meerkat will be twice as much telescope for the same money
Script: Engineer Gundolf Wieching from Germanys biggest research foundation Max Planck Institute for Radio astronomy says they have so much confidence in Meerkat that they are is investing 11 million euro to vastly increase it’s sensitivity
Gundolf 03 35 54 15 The Meerkat will be the most sensitive telescope in the world in these frequencies until SKA 1 comes into operation……so its good to be part of it
Script: But why do we need so many telescopes? Simon Radcliff, technical head for scientific computing explains
Simon Radcliff 06 08 59 Since the dawn of radio astronomy which hasn’t been going that long, less than 100 years. We started off building single dishes and that is the sort of classic lone isolated dish you see the problem with those is as you build them bigger and bigger the cost of those increase exponentially and just the engineering challenge of building a surface that might be 100 diameters and weigh 200 tons and being able to move that around the sky becomes more and more of a challenge and so rather than building one big one, we build lots of small ones and glue them together
Script: The exact location of each antenna is precisely worked out so they can measure many small pieces of the sky and then piece these together to form an image and the more dishes the better the image
Simon 06 09 56 16 so one of the challenges with building lots of dishes is that your data volume goes up with the square of the number of antennae’s so if I build 4 antenna I now have 16 times data than if I just have one antenna. The data deluge is really what comes to dominate modern radio astronomy
Script: The data coming in off the telescopes looks like this, and it’s hard to imagine how it turns into anything useable
Simon Radcliff 06 10 20 08 So it’s a real challenge to take essentially a large amount of noise almost random information that we get from these telescopes and distil that down into something people can use, you can look at , make an image on the screen.
Script: The biggest milestone was designing the superfast computers to handle this mega data
Simon Radcliff 06 26 27 one example of that is the so called roach board which we developed in partnership with Berkley and that really has formed the heart of our correlator for Meerkat, it is now a product we are in the process of commercializing
Script: The Roach Two, an entirely local development, is now being used all over the world in radio astronomy.
Bernie Fanaroff 07 04 08 08 It’s a new global industry called big data . We have huge amounts of data from all kinds of sensors, cell phones or points of sale or traffic sensors …. how do you process that how do you analyse it? Now SKA is at the forefront of that, it’s challenging all of the big IT companies and they want to work with us because it’s an early example of their most challenging problem
LINK 02 27 29 this is the first Meerkat antennae and basically the dish picks up radio waves and converts it into digital signals now that doesn’t mean much to any of us except when I tell you that that digitizer generates the equivalent of 73000 DVDs a day that’s one dvd a second.
Link 02 23 56 all that information needs to be processed and this data centre will eventually handle 10 times the current global internet traffic in one day. Now to do that you are going to need banks and banks of seriously superfast computers
Tracey 02 26 57 what you can see now is we have 50 racks for Meerkat but we are going to be expanding that for another 80 racks for SKA 1... 02 26 24 For Meerkat, this is probably one of the fastest computers in the world …..and that data has to be processed in this very facility and once it is processed it gets crunched up and it gets sent on the optic fibre link to Cape Town
Script: Tracey Cheetham, Infrastructure manager, says it requires vast amounts of fibre optic cable
Tracey02 38 31 if you start looking at the full SKA we have to think of the African partner countries ….all that optic fibre cable will come back here into the Karoo and then go through to Cape Town
Derek So it could probably go a couple times around the world with all that cable,
Tracey At least twice around the world
LINKS 08 14 00 00This is the nerve centre of the project and basically images from those huge dishes at the site nearly 700km away land up here at the screens in the control in Cape Town ready to be observed and analysed by the scientists
Script: Telescope operators monitor the dishes 24/7, operating them remotely from Cape Town and running the scientific surveys requested from around the world. Siya Matshawule, Telescope operator and part time Phd student says the operators are the vital interface between the dishes and the scientists
Siya 07 37 01…., whilst we are also doing the observations you are also monitoring the behaviour of the antennae’s
Script: Siya is one of 600 SKA SA bursary recipients, part of the Government’s master plan to develop young scientists, engineers, electricians and technicians. Hailing from a small village in the Eastern Cape he is today living his dream, .
Siya 07 36 22 as a second year not knowing what to do in physics but when I first took a look at a telescope viewing the moon I was hooked , so being part of the project now is a privilege to make my dreams come true
Script: Prof Santos is Siya’s supervisor at the University of the Western Cape’s newly established Astrophysics Department.
Mario 03 26 08 00 a very important reason for me moving here to SA - it is attracting world leading scientists from many different countries because it’s happening here right it’s not just having access to the data but it’s seeing how this whole thing is being built and being able to participate in the construction process and having a voice about it and which is something which SA has in all this process
Derek 03 28 000 Not just the hosts of this party
Mario No definitely not, leading this party that is what we want
Bernie Fanaroff 06 56 41 we can build the telescope, we can operate the telescope, we can maintain the telescope, and we can use it. I would particularly like to see African scientists winning Nobel prizes, using a telescope in Africa, data processed in Africa, and thinking done in Africa

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): SKA is the best news in SA today, our scientists and engineers are doing us proud, ensuring we lead the international community with the most advance radio telescope facility in the world
metadata.Summary: Now we have won the bid and the politics of SKA have settled what has happened over the last year? The construction of the radio telescopes on Meerkat has begun on the back of what we learnt with the Kat 7 array. The 2nd Meerkat radio telescope is in place and the 3rd is under construction. Our design and construction of the telescopes has been so cost effective and advanced that massive funding has come into South Africa for the construction of the next 61. The Big Data, 1000 terabytes a year which the 64 antenna Meerkat array will generate, requires a slew of astrophysicist and data technicians to process this data. In the light of this massive opportunity over 600 grants have been created to ensure we have the requisite skills to keep it local.
metadata.Further information: The second Meerkat radio telescope is up and the 3rd is under construction, with 61 more on the way. Meerkat will be the most powerful radio telescope in the world and forms part of phase one of SKA. There is no blueprint for these radio telescopes and as scientists and astronomers configure their requirements, the engineers have to come up with the plans on how to construct them in the most cost-effective manner. So far they have done such an excellent and cost-effective job that the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy in Bonn has made R150 million available for South Africa to build and install them. MeerKAT is expected to do transformational science on pulsars and other areas of astronomy, and despite the fact it has only two telescopes up, it has already been used by scientists from around the world. The construction and erection of these telescopes has opened up whole new career paths for local electrical engineering technicians, and the telescopes are now being operated and maintained by a slew of new technicians, freeing the scientists to get on with the work they were trained for. Until recently, the University of the Western Cape had just one post-graduate physicist, now it boasts a whole astronomy department headed up by Professors Russ Taylor and Roy Maartens. They are ensuring that we have the requisite skilled personnel – astrophysicists and data scientists inside South Africa to handle the 1000 terabytes of data which will be gathered per year when the full Meerkat array is up. This phenomenon, known as Big Data, needs astronomers, computer scientists, and mathematicians to decipher it accurately. UWC and universities throughout South Africa now have the funding to develop this capacity locally to ensure it is not outsourced to international service providers. The latest science coming out of the Meerkat telescopes was announced today by UWC and is part of an international cosmology study. They have devised a way of using the Meerkat Radio telescopes to map the radiation from hydrogen atoms to form a 3D map of the universe. These 3D maps will be able to test the limits of General Relativity and the origins of the universe. They can start testing their theories using data gathered from the antennae already in place and expand as the full array is completed. SKA is set to be a giant physics lab for scientists around the world. This insert will also look at what impact some of the technological and engineering advances and data gathered will have on our day to day lives. These advances do not only benefit our understanding of the universe and dark matter, but have practical and commercial implications for our everyday lives.
